name: Erasmus
role: Dutch Renaissance humanist, theologian and editor of the New Testament (c.1466-1536)
summary: Erasmus, the leading Northern humanist, wrote against princes' wars, arguing for peace, arbitration and the Gospel's law of non-retaliation, and for gentle teaching over beating. His satires and dialogues speak in characters' voices, so his settled positions come mainly from the Complaint of Peace and the Education of Children.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: Asked why the 'childish quarrels of princes' are not settled 'by the wisdom and discretion' of bishops, abbots and wise elders instead of war; scholarship records the same arbitration proposal in the Education of a Christian Prince, Dulce Bellum and De Concordia.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Wrote to the young Charles V: 'What is it that alone makes the Prince, if not the consent of those who obey him?' and 'an important part of government is the consent of the people, which was the origin of kings'.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Advised that 'a good Prince will tax least commodities used by the humblest of the people, such as corn, bread, beer, wine, clothing, which are indispensable for the support of life' and condemned the duties and monopolies burdening them; he asks for the lightest burden on necessities and taxes on luxuries, not for an outright exemption, so the answer leans agree only.

gradual-change.rationale: Advised the prince to avoid innovation, since even a change for the better gives offence: 'the intolerable should be corrected, but gradually and tactfully'.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Wrote that 'the State cannot be called tranquil when the populace obeys the Prince's every nod, but rather when it obeys good laws and a Prince who governs himself in accordance with them'.

rehabilitation.rationale: Wrote that wise men condemn laws and officers that only frighten with punishment and do not also entice with rewards or prevent offences, and likewise teachers who only beat.

separated-powers.rationale: Held monarchy best only for a perfect prince, and otherwise that it should be tempered by aristocracy and democracy so that its elements balance one another and do not erupt into tyranny; his editor notes he thought 'certain checks are necessary'.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Advised that if taxation is inevitable the prince should tax imported luxuries 'used only by the wealthy, like fine linen, silks, purple, pepper, spices' so 'only those will be inconvenienced whose fortunes are able to bear it', and that it is good to summon the rich to frugality while the poor must not be reduced to famine.

war-builds-character.rationale: Described war as sent out of hell, as sustained by 'tithes and taxes' that pillage the subjects and as a business whose glory is 'won by and for the dregs of mankind'.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Wrote that the prince should 'avoid excessive inequality of riches', preventing 'the riches of all the people being concentrated in a few persons', citing Plato's citizens neither too rich nor very poor, though not by forcibly depriving anyone.

notes: Erasmus's own prose that is local is mainly Against War (the Complaint of Peace in a Tudor translation with Mackail's introduction) and the Education of Children; the SEP entry reports his arbitration and just-war nuance. Answered: arbitrator-settles-disputes +1, war-builds-character -2, rehabilitation +1 (from his remark that laws and teachers who only punish are condemned by wise men). Added after the integrator's review: the Corbett translation of the Christian Prince chapters III-XI and the Latin scan give consent-of-governed +2 high, cut-consumption-tax +1 medium (lightest tax on necessities, not exemption), tax-the-wealthy +1, widespread-small-property +1, gradual-change +2, promulgated-standing-laws +2 and separated-powers +1 (monarchy tempered by aristocracy and democracy). Not answered: never-kill-self-defence (he grants natural law's permission of self-defence and argues the law of Christ is higher, and in later works concedes war can be legitimate), the Praise of Folly and Colloquies (voices of characters), and his religious views (free will, church authority, Scripture in the vernacular: none matches a bank wording without inference). Themes searched: war, princes, taxes, arbitration, Turks, education, punishment, women, law, religion. Failing the uncertainty rule is the expected outcome.
